newsitem.title: USA: Tensions rise ahead of Chino copper labor talks.
newsitem.headline: Tensions rise ahead of Chino copper labor talks.

text.p: Tensions between Phelps Dodge Corp and United Steelworkers of America have heightened as the company reitereated ahead of labor talks later this month, that its pay freeze offer to Chino copper mine workers stands.

On Wednesday some 1,000 workers and their supporters gathered outside the head office to demonstrate against the company's insistence a pay-freeze at its Chino, New Mexico plant where union members have been without a labor contract since June 30 last year, the USWA said in a statement.
The USWA said it was also protesting against what it called the company's drive to cut healthcare benefits for retirees from the Chino mine, and was denied a meeting with Phelps' CEO Douglas Yearley.

"We cannot let a corporate renegade like Phelps Dodge reduce the living standards for union copper workers or the retired workers who created such fabulous wealth for this corporation," USWA Secretary Treasurer Leo Gerard said.
Phelps Dodge's Treasurer, Tom Foster, told Reuters on Thursday there were only about 150 people at the demonstration, with some 25 of those actual employees.
Yearley was not in the office at the time to speak to union members, but Foster confirmed the company will resume labor talks at Chino on April 24 and 25.
"That's the place to speak," Foster said.
Last August Phelps presented what it termed its final offer for a new labor contract which included no pay hike.
"It's a final offer," Foster reiterated on Thursday.
Healthcare benefits for Chino workers were being brought in line with non-unionized employees, with the benefits tied to number of years with the company, Foster said.

Chino was working at full nameplate capacity and produced 39,700 short tons of contained copper in the first quarter of this year, down 3,000 short tons from the same period last year due to maintenance work at the mill, Foster added.
On Thursday Phelps released its first quarter results with earnings per share at $2.12, down from $2.26 in the same period last year.
First quarter sales were $1.02 billion, up from $1.00 billion.
Yearley said earnings demonstrated "our continued ability to generate significant earnings and cash flow at current copper prices".
